title: Tool Contract v3
description:
The rulebook. A contract turns exactly ONE upstream REST endpoint into an MCP tool, without anyone writing server code. The shape is modeled on the Salla Admin API -- enveloped responses, scoped OAuth, standard pagination -- and Salla is the platform's primary upstream, but the format itself does not tie a contributor to it. One endpoint, one tool, one file.

v2 added `resolve` to a query parameter: a value the AGENT states in stable, human vocabulary that the UPSTREAM wants as something else -- an id that differs per store. The generated code performs the lookup and the substitution, so the translation lives with the binding it belongs to and the agent never learns it.

v3 replaces `interface.response.ui` with an A2UI surface (pinned to v0.9.1). The old block named a display mode and three interpolated strings, which could describe one record and had no way to say what a LIST looks like -- so the collection tools, the majority of the registry, had nothing to render. An A2UI surface says it properly: a component tree with a row template repeated over the result. Breaking, deliberately, and for the same reason v2 was: a client that does not implement A2UI would find no `display` to switch on and render nothing, and the schema id is what lets it refuse a registry it cannot serve correctly instead of serving it wrongly.

contractVersion.description: Semver for THIS contract, not for the upstream API. Bumping it retires the engine's cached generated code.

kind.description: One endpoint per contract. Other kinds (multi-tool packages, openapi-import) are future work -- see the README.

interface.description: What the tool is. Maps 1:1 to the standard MCP tool declaration -- name, title, description, input schema, annotations -- plus the selection hints an agent routes on and the UI hint a client renders with.

name.description: snake_case, verb_noun. Becomes the MCP tool name, so it must be unique across the whole registry.

title.description: Human-readable display name. Served as the MCP tool's title (and as annotations.title to clients that read it there).

description.description: What the tool returns, in one sentence. The agent reads this to route.

whenToUse.description: LLM guidance, positive half: concrete situations where this tool is the right pick. Folded into the tool description and published under _meta, so every MCP client benefits.

whenNotToUse.description: LLM guidance, negative half: situations where the agent should reach for a sibling tool instead. Name the sibling.

annotations.description: MCP's core ToolAnnotations, served to clients verbatim, using MCP's exact field names. They are behavior HINTS to clients and hard facts to our gate: the schema cross-checks them against the HTTP method and the governance layer. All four are required so the author states intent explicitly -- MCP's absent-field defaults (destructiveHint true, openWorldHint true) are for clients, not for reviews. annotations.title is filled from interface.title.

readOnlyHint.description: True when the tool does not modify anything. Drives caching legality and what the agent is told about side effects.

destructiveHint.description: True when the tool may destroy or irreversibly change data (meaningful when readOnlyHint is false). Destructive tools are never cached and always need a human in the loop.

idempotentHint.description: True when calling the tool twice with the same arguments has no additional effect.

openWorldHint.description: True when the tool interacts with an open world of external entities (a live store, the internet); false for closed, self-contained computation.

allOf.$comment: A read-only tool cannot also be destructive.

schema.description: The TOOL's arguments, not the upstream's. Becomes the MCP tool's inputSchema. Expose only the parameters an agent should set -- a contract narrowing a 20-filter endpoint to three useful ones is doing its job.

forbidden.description: Argument names a caller must never be able to supply.

schema.description: Shape of ONE record, unwrapped. Describe what is inside the envelope's data, never the envelope itself -- and for a list endpoint (binding.http.response.collection: true) describe a single item, not the array: the engine returns {items, count, pagination} and shapes each item to this. One rule for detail and list endpoints, so the same category object is described the same way in get_category and list_categories.

a2uiSurface.description:
How a client renders this tool's result, as an A2UI surface (github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui, pinned to v0.9.1 -- the closed production release, so a contract cannot be invalidated by spec drift).

A2UI splits a generative interface into a component tree and a data model, and that split is the same one this repository already draws: the tree is declared HERE, reviewed like every other part of the contract, while the engine supplies the data at call time. The agent never authors components -- an LLM-written interface is exactly what a governed registry exists to prevent -- so what a merchant sees was read by a human before it shipped.

The engine turns this block into `createSurface` + `updateComponents`, and the tool's own result into `updateDataModel`.

catalogId.description: Which component catalog the client renders with. Only A2UI's basic catalog is served today; a catalog is a contract between agent and client, so adding one is a platform decision rather than a per-contract one.

components.description: The component tree, as A2UI's adjacency list: a flat array where parents name their children by id. Exactly one component must have the id `root`. Cross-reference checks in the gate enforce what JSON Schema cannot -- that every child id resolves, and that every data binding names a field this tool actually returns.

id.description: Unique within the surface. One component must be `root`.

component.description: The catalog component to render. Deliberately a subset of A2UI's basic catalog: the interactive components (Button, TextField, CheckBox, ChoicePicker, Slider, DateTimeInput) are NOT allowed, because a control that calls back to the agent would route around governance.execution -- a button that writes is a write that never met its proposal. Presentation only, until actions are governed.

text.description: Text only. The string to show: a literal, a data binding, or a formatting function.

variant.description: Text only. A hint for the base text style.

url.description: Image only. Where the image is fetched from.

children.description: Column, Row and List only. Either a fixed list of child ids, or a template repeated over a list in the data model.

oneOf.description: A fixed set of child component ids.

componentId.description: The component to instantiate once per item.

path.description: Absolute JSON Pointer to the list in the data model, e.g. `/items` for a collection tool.

oneOf.description: A template. Inside the instantiated component, RELATIVE paths (no leading slash) resolve against the current item -- `name`, not `/name`. That is A2UI's deliberate deviation from RFC 6901, and getting it backwards renders every row empty.

child.description: Card only. The id of its single child. Wrap several elements in a Column or Row and name that.

direction.description: List only. How items are laid out.

justify.description: Column and Row only. Arrangement along the main axis.

align.description: Column, Row and List only. Alignment along the cross axis.

weight.description: Relative share of a parent Row or Column, like CSS flex-grow. Only meaningful as a direct child of one.

allOf.$comment: A2UI requires the properties that give a component its content. A Text with no text renders nothing, which is never what the author meant.

a2uiDynamicString.description: A2UI's DynamicString: a literal, a binding to the data model, or a client-side formatting function.

path.description: JSON Pointer into the data model. Leading `/` resolves from the root of the tool's result; no leading slash resolves against the current item inside a template.

a2uiDynamicValue.description: A function argument. A2UI types these individually rather than as strings: `formatCurrency.decimals` is a DynamicNumber and `formatNumber.grouping` a DynamicBoolean, so a literal 2 stays a number instead of becoming "2".

a2uiFunctionCall.description: A pure formatting function the client evaluates while rendering. Restricted to the formatters: they turn a value the tool already returned into something readable, and cannot reach the network or the store. `openUrl` and the boolean operators are excluded -- navigation is an action, not formatting.

call.description: formatCurrency is the one to reach for on Salla money objects: they arrive as {amount, currency}, never as a scalar.

args.description: Arguments to the function. Every formatter takes `value`; each argument is itself a literal or a binding. formatString is the odd one: its `value` is a template string carrying `${/pointer}` expressions inline, rather than a binding object.

returnType.description: Always `string` here: these calls fill a text slot.

allOf.$comment: Each formatter's own required arguments, so a call that could never render is rejected here rather than at the client.

handler.description: A pure function run inside the engine -- no network, no token. For helpers that compute rather than fetch.

httpBinding.description: One REST endpoint on a configured upstream. The base URL is deliberately absent: the engine owns each upstream's host and credentials, so a contract cannot pin production and cannot drift when the upstream moves.

api.description: Which configured upstream the engine should call. Defaults to "salla", the platform's primary upstream. New values require the engine to be configured for that upstream first.

summary.description: The upstream's summary for the endpoint, copied so a reviewer can compare without leaving the diff.

path.description: The endpoint's path, placeholders included, e.g. /coupons/{coupon_id}.

docsUrl.description: Link to the endpoint's documentation (for Salla: docs.salla.dev), so a reviewer can check the contract against its source.

deprecation.description: Upstreams deprecate fields and endpoints on dated notices (Salla does this often). Record it here so the registry can be audited before the sunset.

scopedAuth.description: No secret is ever named in a contract. The engine resolves the credential for the target upstream at call time -- for Salla, the installing merchant's OAuth token. The contract only declares which scopes that credential must carry.

items.description: A scope in the platform's <domain>.read / <domain>.read_write convention (adopted from Salla), e.g. coupons.read.

scopes.description: Scopes the resolved credential must carry for this endpoint. For Salla, copy them from the endpoint's docs; Salla's 401 names the scopes it wanted.

requestParameters.description: How the tool's arguments become an upstream request. `name` is the wire name; `from` is the tool argument feeding it, defaulting to the same string.

path.description: Every {placeholder} in `path` needs an entry. Path parameters are always required.

mode.description: none: send no body. passthrough: every argument not consumed by path or query becomes the JSON body as-is. mapped: only the fields listed below, renamed.

allOf.$comment: mapped without fields sends an empty body, which is never what the author meant.

name.description: The name the upstream expects on the wire, e.g. coupon_id.

from.description: The tool argument to read. Omit when it matches `name`.

style.description: How an array value is serialized. Laravel-style upstreams like Salla use bracket style (status[]=a&status[]=b) unless an endpoint documents otherwise. Scalars use single.

constant.description: A fixed value always sent, instead of reading a tool argument. Use it to pin a filter the agent must not control.

allOf.$comment: A constant is not read from an argument, so pairing it with `from` is contradictory.
A constant is fixed at authoring time; there is nothing to resolve.

valueResolver.description:
Translate what the agent says into what the upstream takes.

Some filters are keyed on values that only exist inside one merchant's store. Salla's order status filter is: a store's id for `shipped` is 1201821018 here and a different number next door, so no agent can know it and no contract can hardcode it. Exposing that id as the tool's argument pushes an upstream implementation detail all the way into the model's vocabulary, and gets the wrong answer whenever the model has not just looked it up.

So the tool takes the stable name -- the slug, `shipped` -- and the generated code turns it into the store's id on the way out, by calling the lookup named here. The interface stays store-independent and the translation stays in the binding, beside the other things the agent never sees: the host, the token, the array serialization.

The endpoint is written out rather than read from the sibling at runtime, because the generated module is self-contained and has no registry. The gate holds the two in agreement, so the duplication cannot drift.

contract.description: The lookup this resolver calls. It must also appear in this contract's `dependencies`, must be read-only, and its scopes must already be covered by this contract's -- a resolver cannot reach further into a store than the tool it serves.

path.description: The lookup endpoint's path, which the gate checks against the named contract's own binding. No placeholders: a resolver runs before the request is built and has no arguments of its own.

dataPath.description: Dotted path to the records inside the lookup's envelope. For Salla, `data`.

matchOn.description: Dotted field paths on a looked-up record to compare the caller's value against, in order, case-insensitively. More than one because a merchant's word may sit in any of them: `slug` holds 'shipped', `name` holds the store's own label -- often Arabic -- and `translations.en.name` holds the English one.

sendField.description: Dotted path to the value actually sent upstream once a record matches, e.g. `id`.

onMiss.description: What happens to a value that matches no record. `error` fails the call naming the value and what the store does have. `drop` removes it, and has to be chosen deliberately: a filter that quietly disappears is answered by the upstream with everything, which reads as a result rather than as a failure. That is the exact bug this whole feature exists to end, so the default is never silence.

responseEnvelope.description: Salla-style upstreams wrap every response in an envelope ({status, success, data}) and add a pagination object on lists. The engine unwraps using this, so the agent and the UI see the payload rather than the wrapper.

dataPath.description: Dotted path to the payload inside the envelope. For Salla, always `data`.

collection.description: True when the payload is an array. Drives list rendering and tells the agent this returns many rows.

pagination.description: standard means the upstream returns a pagination object alongside the data (for Salla: {count, total, perPage, currentPage, totalPages}).

successStatuses.description: Which HTTP statuses count as success. Salla, for instance, returns 201 on some creates and 202 on deletes.

allOf.$comment: A paginated response is a collection by definition; saying otherwise misleads the agent about what it gets back.

errorEnvelope.description: How this endpoint fails. Salla-style upstreams return the same envelope on failure -- {status, success: false, error: {code, message, fields?}} -- and document the statuses per endpoint. Declaring them lets the engine surface a real reason to the agent instead of a raw dump, and lets the agent tell the user 'no category with that id' rather than 'request failed'. Success and failure cannot overlap by construction: successStatuses is 2xx, these are 4xx/5xx.

messagePath.description: Dotted path to the human-readable failure reason inside the error envelope. For Salla, error.message.

fieldsPath.description: Dotted path to per-field validation errors, when the upstream returns them (Salla's 422 shape: error.fields maps field paths to message arrays). Omit when it has none.

statuses.description: The failure statuses this endpoint is documented to return, each with what it means HERE -- a 404 on a detail endpoint means the id was wrong, which is worth saying precisely.

meaning.description: What this status means for THIS endpoint, written for the agent to relay to a user, e.g. 'no category exists with this id'.

retryable.description: Whether the engine may retry the call unchanged. When omitted the engine decides by class: 429 and 5xx retryable, other 4xx not. Declare it only to override or make the upstream's documented behavior explicit.

validation.description: Guards compiled into the generated code, so a malformed argument fails locally instead of costing a round trip and an upstream 422.

match.description: Regex the argument value must match.

dependencies.description: Other contracts this tool depends on -- a lookup that must happen first, a session another binding establishes. Declared for the reviewer and the agent's documentation; the POC engine does not resolve or order them yet.

contract.description: The tool name of the contract this one depends on.

reason.description: Why the dependency exists, e.g. 'coupon ids come from list_coupons'.

governance.description: How the tool is allowed to run -- OUR policy layer, which MCP leaves open. Cross-checked by the schema against interface.annotations and the HTTP method, so policy cannot quietly disagree with declared behavior.

allOf.$comment: propose-apply exists so a human can approve. Requiring the mode without the approval is a governance hole.
A cacheable result with no TTL never expires, so stale store data would be served indefinitely.

annotationGovernanceRules.$comment: Cross-layer rules tying the MCP annotations to the governance policy. A hint that lies to clients while policy quietly does the opposite is worse than either mistake alone.

allOf.$comment: A destructive tool must never be cacheable. Caching a write is a correctness bug, not a preference.

Only a read-only tool may be cacheable. Without this, a write could be marked cacheable and merely happen not to be cached because the engine checks readOnlyHint too -- an invariant enforced in one place and silently contradicted in another.

methodGovernanceRules.$comment: Cross-layer rules tying the HTTP verb and its scopes to the MCP annotations. These catch the mistakes that matter: a write tool marked read-only would be cached and served stale, and a read tool asking for read_write hands the store more access than the job needs.

allOf.$comment: GET is a read. Marking it otherwise disables caching for no reason and misleads the agent.
POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE change store data. None of them is read-only.
DELETE removes real data. It is destructive whatever the author felt about it, and always gets a human in the loop.
Least privilege: a read-only tool must not request a read_write scope. Grants are made per app installation, so an over-broad ask gives the whole app more power over a store than this tool needs.
The converse: a tool that writes cannot do it with a read-only scope. The upstream would reject the call at runtime; better to reject the contract at review time.
